_doc: Retrieval oracle. Each case is a query a game-builder would actually type,
plus the set of assets that would be a correct answer.
Expectations are path globs over 'pack:path', derived from the corpus's own
naming -- objective facts a human can check by listing files -- never from
this index's ranking, which would make the eval circular.
'*' matches any characters including '/'. A case passes at k if any returned
asset in the top k matches any expect pattern.
Metric: recall@10. Run: assets eval
Two kinds of case:
lexical  - the answer's filename contains the query words. Filename
matching wins these by construction; they check the index
does not regress, not that enrichment helps.
semantic - scoped to 1-bit-platformer, whose files are named tile_0000
.. tile_0195 and carry no meaning at all. No amount of
filename matching can answer these. Labels were established
by rendering a contact sheet and looking at it, then
cross-checking against the independently-produced legacy
descriptions; only cases where both agreed were kept.
Ground truth is widened only after rendering the candidate and confirming
by eye that it answers the query. A lexical case's expectations were first
written when only filename-matched assets could be found; as opaque-named
assets gain descriptions they legitimately outrank those, and the suite has
to learn the new correct answers rather than score them as failures.
Never widen an expectation to make a number look better.
2026-09-06: widened from 69 to ~304 cases. Three kinds now:
lexical  - filename says it; spread across ~50 packs the old suite never touched
semantic - opaque filenames; ground truth is a description that was AUDITED
against the pixels (assets.audited=1), from four packs
intent   - a sentence a builder would actually type, with permissive but
honest expectations. These are the shape of real queries and the
old suite had none.
All still authored by the same mind that wrote the descriptions; a third
written by someone else remains the outstanding gap.
